posts.name: Animus
posts.cooked:
Some other things I gleaned from the demo and jotted down. I jotted it down in a doc but forgot about it until tonight, so I'm sharing now:

Scenes

three scene feature categories: threats, obstacles, and challenges

Threats hit back. often tied to a villain (as spoken by the GM). Threats were individual dice (d6, d8, etc.). If your attack result > die type, eliminate threat, otherwise step down the die (d8->d6, d6->, d4->defeated). 

unresolved obstacles increase the scene stress, in the example it was one point per obstacle.

challenges take multiple successes to overcome. if they are not resolved by the time the track gets to "out," bad things happen.

 

Scene zone colors & stress

Green: 2 or 3 points

Yellow: points = # obstacles

Red: 2 or 3

Out

Laid out like:

G:OOO | Y: OOOO | R: OOO | Out

Mark 1 circle per obstacle left at the end of the round.

 

Does that help?

posts.name: Animus
posts.cooked:
eviltoon:

Awesome notes, man! Thank you. That totally changes how I interpreted Arenson's explanation of the scene dice. I must've just read that one wrong-- but this is interesting. What would a "challenge" be, versus an obstacle? Is it just the increased (well, challenge) to overcome it-- so instead of a small fire, it's a roaring fire burning down a building? Or what? Thanks for the help to flesh this out some!

An obstacle only required one success to overcome, and it increases the urgency of the scene. E.g. a small localized fire.

A challenge takes multiple successes to overcome, does not increase the urgency of the scene, but has a consequence when the scene gets to the Out (Black) zone. E.g. A blazing fire which threatened to burn the building down and everyone in it.

(Side Note: Christopher called the system GYRO: Green,  Yellow,  Red,  Out)   

In the demo, the challenge we had to  get three or four successes to beat it. 

Oh yeah, initiative worked mostly like MHR, but you probably figured that out.

posts.name: Pydro
posts.cooked: What has been the philosophy regarding party balance? For SotM, the idea is that any team can take on anybody, theoretically, and there isn’t this idea of needinh a particular role, like a healer.

posts.name: TheChattyDM
posts.cooked:
We didn't go for an "established roles" type of philosophy. Many SotM characters are based on superheroic tropes we recognize and can tap easily into. We wanted that too.

Much like the card and tactics game, characters perform through finding creative ways to tap into what they do best (as driven by dice traits, kickers and principles) and then discovering synergies between characters. For instance, picking the order of who acts next during a turn can be key in overcoming a specific type of obstacle or beating a specific type of villain.

So no we're not aiming specifically at "balanced characters" but more making all of them, including the ones you'll design, fun and challenging to play at the table. In that, our Marvel Heroic RPG roots kinda show.

posts.name: Sonvar
posts.cooked: What storyline did you go through at Gencon?

posts.name: TheChattyDM
posts.cooked:
Good question (as I wrote the adventure, tee hee)

As Grand Warlord Voss planned to invade Wagner Mars Base, he sent Gene Bound humans to infiltrate the Wagner Space Centre in the outskirts of Megalopolis. He needed them to create a diversion during the unveiling of an experimental wormhole portal so they could find and recuperate the codes to deactivate the base' Self-Destruct sequence.

The heroes all attended the unveiling in various roles the players chose to play. For instance, in almost all cases, Tachyon played a role as a scientist on the project. Wraith often attended as Maya Montgomery, among the VIPs.

The portal exploded upon activation (sabotage!) and a LOT of things went wrong at the same time, giving each character more than one problem to act upon. So it was what I call a "complex scene" where combat and non combat threats had to be dealt with before the scene went critical (i.e. went passed RED) and everyone got sucked in the collapsing portal.

Then, all heroes were sent to Mars to kick out Voss who had launched his assault of the base. This was a more straightforward combat encounter using both a supervillain, many minions and the environment itself (who also as a turn, rolls dice and has various kickers that also double as costs for when thinmgs invariably go wrong).

posts.name: TheChattyDM
posts.cooked:
Well, I'd be lying through my teeth if we didn't come out and say we were inspired by our previous work and some of the most influencial roleplaying games of the last decade. So you'll see some Apocalypse, Fate, Marvel and some D&D in there.

I openly said before that I've long wanted to have a game that not only had "success as a cost" as part of its core mechanic, but one where the burden of coming up with costs didn't solely reside on the shoulders of an already very busy game master. Dave, Cam and I came up with things that went far above and beyond my initial expectations.

On to the actual questions then

1) The back of the sheet explained how Reactions worked, what happened when you rolled triples (score XP), what were spotlight callbacks (when you called back to previous adventure to offset a minor cost or max a die), how heroic principles worked and the rules for recovery. I guess I could attach it if the forum allows PDFs. I'll talk to Craig about this. It's kinda public after all. Although seeing you champ at the bits for it is also fun. :)

2) You guys have worked out how minions work. We have rules for more important minions (we call them lieutenants) too. Villains work like simplified heroes. They have just three dice traits and colour coded kickers (Green and Red, emulating when they 'flip"). For example, Voss, while in green mode summons minions and makes them stronger. While in red, he attacks violently and summons big ass starship minions (with special rules).

3) Thanks!

4) Here, we call them Boisson Gazeuse in formal French (or Carbonated Drinks) and Liqueur in common French (liquor, weirdly enough). In English, it's soda, although we almost always refer to the product's actual brand. And Pepsi outsells coke here... one of the reasons Pepsi is used as (one of the many) cultural slurs to refer to us French Canadians.  

Hope that helped.
